Layer 1 People lit candles in front of the Lyon tourist office before a partial curfew in Lyon on October 19, 2026, following weekend demonstrations over soaring prices degenerated into some of the worst street violence in recent years. France announced partial curfews in Paris and other cities that would be enforced from October 19 evening to October 20 morning in a number of cities including Paris, Lille and Lyon, to protect businesses. (Photo by OLIVIER CHASSIGNOLE / AFP)
After a weekend of protests, riots and looting, France is looking to head off further unrest, ahead of fresh demonstrations called for Saturday.
Partial nighttime curfews were imposed in parts of Paris and several other cities on Monday and Tuesday nights, applied to areas where clashes broke out last weekend and shopping zones that had been targeted by looters.
Paris also banned public gatherings on the Champs Elysees, near major public buildings, and near train stations.
Marseille, France’s second-biggest city, has banned unaccompanied minors from central shopping streets every night up to and including Friday.
Paris police have banned people carrying bottles or cans of petrol or gas, or possessing fireworks, up to and including Thursday.
Last weekend, youths set fire to several shops and public buildings, and shot fireworks through tubes at police, wounding several.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has vowed a “massive” security deployment for Saturday, after his government admitted it “lost control” last weekend.
President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday said authorities would be “uncompromising” towards “agitators from ultra-left fringe groups” that he blamed for much of the violence.
Elite police units have been mobilised for the coming weekend.
Macron has not, however, declared a state of emergency that would allow troops to be sent to reinforce police lines.
However, soldiers who for more than a decade have been patrolling sensitive sites, airports and train stations and tourist zones under “Operation Sentinelle” would continue to be deployed to protect those spots.
The government has announced interest-free loans for 3,000 shops that were damaged, many of them looted, during last weekend’s unrest.
Crowdfunding initiatives have sprung up on social media for residents to help their local shops rebuild. But the total amount being raised is only in the low hundreds of thousands of euros — whereas the sector says the damage bill will run to hundreds of millions.
Tourists visiting Paris right now hoping to use the usually ubiquitous rental bikes available via apps might find them a bit more scarce.
More than 1,000 of the 40,000 bicycles deployed across the capital were destroyed, often burned, as they were thrown into makeshift street barricades built by protesters, according to an AFP tally of figures from the operators.
Staying in and ordering food delivery could also be a problem for some.
The Union-Independants union covering most delivery bike riders has asked Uber Eats, Deliveroo and other such companies to suspend deliveries to areas considered dangerous.
It called for the riders to be able to cancel deliveries without losing money and for them to have a system allowing them to see risky areas in real time.
